title: Code Signing
summary: Code signing applies a cryptographic signature to an executable, script, installer, driver or container image so a verifier can confirm who produced it and whether it changed afterwards. The publisher signs a hash of the artifact with a private key, and the operating system, package manager or downloader validates that signature against a trusted certificate chain before allowing the code to run or install. It appears throughout software distribution pipelines, application control policies, driver signing requirements, mobile application stores and script execution policies. Evidence includes signed binaries carrying publisher names, signature validation events, blocked execution of unsigned or modified files, timestamp and certificate records, and alerts when a valid but unexpected signing certificate appears. Signing is not a verdict on safety: a signed artifact can still be malicious, and stolen or misused signing keys remain a recurring supply chain problem.

beginner.definition: Code signing puts a digital signature on a program or script. The signature shows who made the file and whether anyone changed it since. Your computer can check the signature before it runs the code. If the check fails, the file is blocked or you see a warning.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without a check, your computer cannot tell a real update from a fake one. Attackers often wrap harmful code in a familiar looking installer. A signature makes tampering visible, because even one changed byte breaks the check. This protects software updates, drivers and scripts in your environment. Remember that a valid signature proves origin, not good behaviour.
howItWorks: The publisher creates a hash, a short fingerprint calculated from the file contents.
The publisher signs that fingerprint with a private key that only they hold.
The signed file and its certificate travel together to your computer for checking.
Your system recalculates the fingerprint and checks the signature with the public key.
It also checks whether the certificate chain leads to a trusted authority.
If everything matches the code runs, and if not, policy blocks it or warns you.
beginner.example: Think of a passport at an airport border. The document carries a stamp that officers can verify, and the photo must match the traveller. Anyone can print a booklet at home, but the security features and the official stamp are hard to copy. A valid passport still does not promise the traveller is honest, it only proves who they are. Code signing works the same way: the stamp proves the file came from a named publisher and was not altered. Officers still watch behaviour, because a real passport can belong to a troublemaker.
takeaways: A signature proves origin and integrity, not that the code is safe.
Protect private signing keys, because a stolen key signs anything.
Enforce signing at execution time, not only when a file is downloaded.

objectives: Explain how a digital signature is created and verified for a file.
Describe where code signing is enforced in a normal organisation.
Identify the evidence left when a signature check fails or is bypassed.
Explain why a stolen signing key is a supply chain risk.
Distinguish integrity and origin from the safety of the code.
